```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

cps_df = pd.read_csv("data/cps_gender_pay_gap.csv")

# Vienna hotels, same filters as Weeks 4 and 5
hotels = pd.read_csv("data/hotels_vienna.csv")
hotels = hotels[(hotels.accommodation_type == 'Hotel') & (hotels.city_actual == 'Vienna')
                & hotels.stars.between(3, 4) & (hotels.price <= 600)].copy()
hotels['ln_price'] = np.log(hotels['price'])
hotels['dist_b1'] = np.maximum(hotels['distance'] - 1, 0)
hotels['dist_b4'] = np.maximum(hotels['distance'] - 4, 0)
hotels['rating_b35'] = np.maximum(hotels['rating'] - 3.5, 0)
hotel_model = smf.ols('ln_price ~ distance + dist_b1 + dist_b4 + rating + rating_b35 + C(stars)',
                      data=hotels).fit(cov_type='HC1')
hotels['resid'] = hotel_model.resid

# Building the hotels model up one block at a time, for the comparison table
_hf = ['ln_price ~ distance',
       'ln_price ~ distance + dist_b1 + dist_b4',
       'ln_price ~ distance + dist_b1 + dist_b4 + rating + rating_b35',
       'ln_price ~ distance + dist_b1 + dist_b4 + rating + rating_b35 + C(stars)']
hotel_models = [smf.ols(_f, data=hotels).fit(cov_type='HC1') for _f in _hf]
_deals = [set(hotels.assign(_r=_m.resid).nsmallest(5, '_r')['hotel_id']) for _m in hotel_models]
hotel_overlap = len(_deals[0] & _deals[3])
_st = hotel_models[3].f_test("C(stars)[T.3.5] = 0, C(stars)[T.4.0] = 0")
hotel_stars_f = round(float(np.squeeze(_st.fvalue)), 1)
hotel_deals = hotels.nsmallest(5, 'resid')[['hotel_id', 'price', 'resid', 'distance', 'stars', 'rating']]
```

# Worked example {background-color="#2d6a4f"}
## The gender pay gap

---

## Understanding the gender difference in earnings

- In the USA (2014), women tend to earn about 20% less than men
- Aim 1: find patterns that help us understand the gender gap, focusing on how it interacts with age
- Aim 2: think about whether there is a causal link from being female to being paid less

## Set up

- 2014 census data
  - Age between 24 and 64
  - Self-employed excluded as earning are difficult to measure
  - Include those who reported 20 hours or more as their usual weekly time worked
- Employees with a graduate degree
- Use log hourly earnings (lw) as the dependent variable
- Use gender and add age as an explanatory variable

## Setting up the question

The simple model of the relation between earnings and gender is: 

$$\ln w^E = \alpha + \beta\, female$$

Let's include age as well: 

$$\ln w^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 female + \beta_2 age $$
We can also regress age on female, to see how the two are related: 
$$ age^E = \gamma + \delta female$$

## Adding age as a confounder

::: {.big-code}
```{.python}
smf.ols('ln_wage ~ female + age', data=cps_df).fit(cov_type='HC1')
```
:::

```{python}
#| output: asis
def _stars(p):
    return "***" if p < 0.01 else "**" if p < 0.05 else "*" if p < 0.1 else ""

_m1  = smf.ols('ln_wage ~ female', data=cps_df).fit(cov_type='HC1')
_m2  = smf.ols('ln_wage ~ female + age', data=cps_df).fit(cov_type='HC1')
_aux = smf.ols('age ~ female', data=cps_df).fit(cov_type='HC1')

_rows = [
    ("female", f"{_m1.params['female']:.3f}{_stars(_m1.pvalues['female'])}",
               f"{_m2.params['female']:.3f}{_stars(_m2.pvalues['female'])}",
               f"{_aux.params['female']:.3f}{_stars(_aux.pvalues['female'])}"),
    ("age", "", f"{_m2.params['age']:.3f}{_stars(_m2.pvalues['age'])}", ""),
    ("Constant", f"{_m1.params['Intercept']:.3f}{_stars(_m1.pvalues['Intercept'])}",
                 f"{_m2.params['Intercept']:.3f}{_stars(_m2.pvalues['Intercept'])}",
                 f"{_aux.params['Intercept']:.3f}{_stars(_aux.pvalues['Intercept'])}"),
    ("Observations", f"{int(_m1.nobs):,}", f"{int(_m2.nobs):,}", f"{int(_aux.nobs):,}"),
    ("R²", f"{_m1.rsquared:.3f}", f"{_m2.rsquared:.3f}", f"{_aux.rsquared:.3f}"),
]
print("| Variable | (1) ln wage | (2) ln wage | (3) age |")
print("|---|---|---|---|")
for label, c1, c2, c3 in _rows:
    print(f"| {label} | {c1} | {c2} | {c3} |")
```

Column (3) is the $age$-on-$female$ regression — women in this sample are, on average, younger than men.

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Checking the OVB formula

$$\beta-\beta_1=\delta\beta_2$$
which can be easily calculated

```{python}
#| output: asis
_diff = _m1.params['female'] - _m2.params['female']
_prod = _aux.params['female'] * _m2.params['age']
print(f"- $\\beta-\\beta_1 = {_m1.params['female']:.3f}-({_m2.params['female']:.3f}) = {_diff:.4f}$")
print(f"- $\\delta\\beta_2 = {_aux.params['female']:.3f}\\times{_m2.params['age']:.3f} \\approx {_prod:.4f}$")
```

::: {.fragment}
**Age is a confounder here — but a weak one.** Women in the data are somewhat younger, and younger employees earn less regardless of gender — so a small slice (about 1 percentage point of the 20%, roughly 5% of the whole gap) is attributable to the age difference, not gender itself.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Looking at the age distribution {.smaller}


Let's plot the difference in the age distribution of employees with graduate degrees. 



::: {.small-code}
```{.python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
import numpy as np

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
colors = {0: '#2d6a4f', 1: '#457b9d'}
labels = {0: 'Male', 1: 'Female'}
age_grid = np.linspace(cps_df['age'].min(), cps_df['age'].max(), 200)

for f in [0, 1]:
    ages = cps_df.loc[cps_df.female == f, 'age']
    kde = gaussian_kde(ages)
    ax.plot(age_grid, kde(age_grid), color=colors[f], linewidth=2.5, label=labels[f])

ax.set_xlabel('Age (years)')
ax.set_ylabel('Density')
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
```
:::

## The age distribution, plotted



```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
import numpy as np

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
_colors = {0: '#2d6a4f', 1: '#457b9d'}
_labels = {0: 'Male', 1: 'Female'}
_age_grid = np.linspace(cps_df['age'].min(), cps_df['age'].max(), 200)

for _f in [0, 1]:
    _ages = cps_df.loc[cps_df.female == _f, 'age']
    _kde = gaussian_kde(_ages)
    ax.plot(_age_grid, _kde(_age_grid), color=_colors[_f], linewidth=2.5, label=_labels[_f])

ax.set_xlabel('Age (years)')
ax.set_ylabel('Density')
ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.spines[['top', 'right']].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Among graduate-degree holders, the proportion of *women* drops noticeably after age 45, and again after 55 — men's age distribution stays close to uniform from 30 to 55.

::: {.instructions-box}
Two explanations are consistent with this pattern: fewer women completed graduate degrees in earlier decades, or fewer older women are currently employed. 
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Should we consider a non-linear relationship? {.smaller}

::: {.big-code}
```{.python}
smf.ols('ln_wage ~ female + age + I(age**2) + I(age**3) + I(age**4)', data=cps_df).fit(cov_type='HC1')
```
:::

```{python}
#| output: asis
_m3 = smf.ols('ln_wage ~ female + age + I(age**2)', data=cps_df).fit(cov_type='HC1')
_m4 = smf.ols('ln_wage ~ female + age + I(age**2) + I(age**3) + I(age**4)', data=cps_df).fit(cov_type='HC1')

_female_row = " | ".join(f"{m.params['female']:.3f}{_stars(m.pvalues['female'])}" for m in [_m1,_m2,_m3,_m4])
_age_row    = " | ".join([""] + [f"{m.params['age']:.3f}{_stars(m.pvalues['age'])}" for m in [_m2,_m3,_m4]])
_age2_row   = " | ".join(["", ""] + [f"{m.params['I(age ** 2)']:.3f}{_stars(m.pvalues['I(age ** 2)'])}" for m in [_m3,_m4]])
_age34_row  = " | ".join(["", "", "", f"✓{_stars(min(_m4.pvalues['I(age ** 3)'], _m4.pvalues['I(age ** 4)']))}"])

print("| | (1) | (2) | (3) | (4) |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|")
print(f"| female | {_female_row} |")
print(f"| age | {_age_row} |")
print(f"| age² | {_age2_row} |")
print(f"| age³, age⁴ | {_age34_row} |")
print(f"| R² | {_m1.rsquared:.3f} | {_m2.rsquared:.3f} | {_m3.rsquared:.3f} | {_m4.rsquared:.3f} |")
```

::: {.fragment}
```{python}
#| output: asis
_chain = " → ".join(f"{m.params['female']:.3f}" for m in [_m1,_m2,_m3,_m4])
print(f"The **female** coefficient barely moves at all — {_chain} — while R² keeps climbing with every extra polynomial term. But: **more variables always raise R², but that's not the same as changing the story.** Here, no matter how flexibly age is modelled, the gender gap doesn't budge.")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Does the gap even have the same slope for both?

::: {.big-code}
```{.python}
smf.ols('ln_wage ~ age * female', data=cps_df).fit(cov_type='HC1')
```
:::

```{python}
#| output: asis
_women = smf.ols('ln_wage ~ age', data=cps_df[cps_df.female==1]).fit(cov_type='HC1')
_men   = smf.ols('ln_wage ~ age', data=cps_df[cps_df.female==0]).fit(cov_type='HC1')
_inter = smf.ols('ln_wage ~ age * female', data=cps_df).fit(cov_type='HC1')

print("| | Women only | Men only | Pooled, interacted |")
print("|---|---|---|---|")
print(f"| female | | | {_inter.params['female']:.3f}{_stars(_inter.pvalues['female'])} |")
print(f"| age | {_women.params['age']:.3f}{_stars(_women.pvalues['age'])} | {_men.params['age']:.3f}{_stars(_men.pvalues['age'])} | {_inter.params['age']:.3f}{_stars(_inter.pvalues['age'])} |")
print(f"| female × age | | | {_inter.params['age:female']:.3f}{_stars(_inter.pvalues['age:female'])} |")
```

::: {.instructions-box}
```{python}
#| output: asis
print(f"The **female** coefficient in the pooled model is close to zero ({_inter.params['female']:.3f}, not even the whole 20% gap). Does this mean the gender gap has disappeared? What does the interaction term tell you that the dummy alone doesn't?")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Interactions and non-linearities together

Let's consider two models

$$ \ln w^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 age + \beta_2 female + \beta_3 female \times age $$

and adding age as non-linear

$$ \ln w^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 age + \beta_2 age^2 + \beta_3 age^3 + \beta_4 age^4 \\ + \beta_5 female + \beta_6 female \times age + \beta_7 female \times age ^2 \\ + \beta_8 female \times age^3 + \beta_9 female \times age^4 $$

## Interactions and non-linearities together

Running the fully flexible version — 4th-order polynomial in age, interacted with gender — reveals the real pattern:

```{python}
#| output: asis
import numpy as np

_full = smf.ols(
    'ln_wage ~ female*age + female:I(age**2) + female:I(age**3) + female:I(age**4) '
    '+ age + I(age**2) + I(age**3) + I(age**4)', data=cps_df
).fit(cov_type='HC1')

def _gap_pct(age):
    p0 = _full.predict(pd.DataFrame({'age': [age], 'female': [0]})).iloc[0]
    p1 = _full.predict(pd.DataFrame({'age': [age], 'female': [1]})).iloc[0]
    return (np.exp(p1 - p0) - 1) * 100

_g25, _g30, _g40, _g50, _g60 = (_gap_pct(a) for a in [25, 30, 40, 50, 60])

print(f"- The gap is around **{min(abs(_g25), abs(_g30)):.0f}–{max(abs(_g25), abs(_g30)):.0f}%** between ages 25 and 30")
print(f"- Rises to **{abs(_g40):.0f}%** by 40, and **{abs(_g50):.0f}%** by 50")
print(f"- {'Tapers slightly' if abs(_g60) < abs(_g50) else 'Keeps rising'} after 60 (**{abs(_g60):.0f}%**)")
```

::: {.fragment}
A single "female" coefficient could never have told this story. The gap isn't a fixed number — it **grows through most of a career** and only the full interacted, non-linear model shows that shape.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Predicting the gap by age {.smaller}

::: {.small-code}
```{.python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

age_grid = np.linspace(25, 65, 50)

def predict_band(model, ages, female):
    X = pd.DataFrame({'age': ages, 'female': female})
    return model.get_prediction(X).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), sharey=True)
panels = [(axes[0], inter, 'Linear interaction'),
          (axes[1], full, '4th-order polynomial interaction')]

for ax, model, title in panels:
    for female, color, label in [(0, '#2d6a4f', 'Male'), (1, '#457b9d', 'Female')]:
        band = predict_band(model, age_grid, female)
        ax.plot(age_grid, band['mean'], color=color, label=label)
        ax.fill_between(age_grid, band['mean_ci_lower'], band['mean_ci_upper'], color=color, alpha=0.15)
    ax.set_xlabel('Age (years)')
    ax.set_title(title)

axes[0].set_ylabel('ln(earnings per hour)')
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
```
:::

## The gap by age, plotted

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

_age_grid2 = np.linspace(25, 65, 50)

def _predict_band(model, ages, female):
    X = pd.DataFrame({'age': ages, 'female': female})
    return model.get_prediction(X).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), sharey=True)
_panels = [(axes[0], _inter, 'Linear interaction'),
           (axes[1], _full, '4th-order polynomial interaction')]

for ax, model, title in _panels:
    for female, color, label in [(0, '#2d6a4f', 'Male'), (1, '#457b9d', 'Female')]:
        band = _predict_band(model, _age_grid2, female)
        ax.plot(_age_grid2, band['mean'], color=color, label=label)
        ax.fill_between(_age_grid2, band['mean_ci_lower'], band['mean_ci_upper'], color=color, alpha=0.15)
    ax.set_xlabel('Age (years)')
    ax.set_title(title)

axes[0].set_ylabel('ln(earnings per hour)')
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.instructions-box}
Both panels show predicted ln(earnings) by age and gender, with 95% confidence bands. The linear-interaction panel forces the gap to widen at a constant rate; the polynomial panel lets it curve — women's predicted earnings flatten and dip after around 45, exactly where the age-distribution wrinkle showed fewer women in the data to estimate from precisely.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## What we still can't say

- Multiple regression got us closer to a fair comparison — same age, same education
- It **cannot** rule out that broader gender inequality (career interruptions, occupational sorting, negotiation norms) drives part of what's left
- We can't prove how much of the remaining gap is labour-market discrimination specifically — there's too much unmeasured heterogeneity
- And we haven't ruled out **selection** or **bad conditioning variables** either

::: {.fragment}
This is the honest ceiling of conditioning on observables. Getting further needs a different kind of design — which is where the module goes from Week 9 onward.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

# A practical detour {background-color="#2d6a4f"}
## Presenting a regression table

---

## What actually belongs in a table

- **In a presentation**: suppress coefficients nobody's there to discuss — keep the variables that matter for the story
- **In a paper**: show more, but mainly as a sanity check — do the control-variable coefficients make sense?
- **Always check N** — if it's supposed to be the same sample across columns, the observation count should match exactly
- **R² is usually enough.** You don't need every fit statistic software offers by default

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Building the table in Python {.smaller}

The four gender-gap models side by side, coefficients with stars, standard errors underneath:

::: {.mid-code}
```{.python}
def stars(p):
    return "***" if p < 0.01 else "**" if p < 0.05 else "*" if p < 0.1 else ""

models = {'(1)': m1, '(2)': m2, '(3)': m3, '(4)': m4}
rows = {}
for name, label in [('female', 'Female'), ('age', 'Age')]:
    rows[label] = {k: f"{m.params[name]:.3f}{stars(m.pvalues[name])}" if name in m.params else ""
                   for k, m in models.items()}
    rows[label + ' SE'] = {k: f"({m.bse[name]:.3f})" if name in m.params else "" for k, m in models.items()}
rows['N'] = {k: f"{int(m.nobs):,}" for k, m in models.items()}
rows['R²'] = {k: f"{m.rsquared:.3f}" for k, m in models.items()}
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).T.to_markdown())
```
:::

```{python}
#| output: asis
_models = {'(1)': _m1, '(2)': _m2, '(3)': _m3, '(4)': _m4}
print("| | (1) | (2) | (3) | (4) |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|")
for _n, _lab in [('female', 'Female'), ('age', 'Age')]:
    print("| " + _lab + " | " + " | ".join(f"{m.params[_n]:.3f}{_stars(m.pvalues[_n])}" if _n in m.params else "" for m in _models.values()) + " |")
    print("| | " + " | ".join(f"({m.bse[_n]:.3f})" if _n in m.params else "" for m in _models.values()) + " |")
print("| N | " + " | ".join(f"{int(m.nobs):,}" for m in _models.values()) + " |")
print("| R² | " + " | ".join(f"{m.rsquared:.3f}" for m in _models.values()) + " |")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;"}
Models (3) and (4) add age², and age² to age⁴. Robust standard errors in brackets. `to_markdown()` needs the `tabulate` package, already installed in Colab.
:::

# Worked example {background-color="#2d6a4f"}
## Closing the hotels thread: finding a good deal

---

## Back to Vienna, with everything we now have {.smaller}

In Week 4 we went looking for a good hotel deal with one x at a time. Now we can put it all in one model:

$$\ln(price)^E = f(\text{distance spline}) + f(\text{rating spline}) + \beta_{3.5\,stars} + \beta_{4\,stars}$$

- Distance: piecewise linear spline, knots at 1 and 4 miles
- Rating: piecewise linear spline, knot at 3.5
- Stars: dummies for 3.5★ and 4★ (reference: 3★)

::: {.mid-code}
```{.python}
hotels['dist_b1'] = np.maximum(hotels['distance'] - 1, 0)
hotels['dist_b4'] = np.maximum(hotels['distance'] - 4, 0)
hotels['rating_b35'] = np.maximum(hotels['rating'] - 3.5, 0)

model = smf.ols('ln_price ~ distance + dist_b1 + dist_b4 + rating + rating_b35 + C(stars)',
                data=hotels).fit(cov_type='HC1')
```
:::

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(f"R² = **{hotel_model.rsquared:.2f}**, against 0.16 for Week 4's straight line in distance alone.")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10, hotels-vienna dataset
:::

## Comparing the hotel models {.smaller}

The same table code as before, now building the hotels model up one block at a time:

::: {.small-code}
```{.python}
m1 = smf.ols('ln_price ~ distance', data=hotels).fit(cov_type='HC1')
m2 = smf.ols('ln_price ~ distance + dist_b1 + dist_b4', data=hotels).fit(cov_type='HC1')
m3 = smf.ols('ln_price ~ distance + dist_b1 + dist_b4 + rating + rating_b35', data=hotels).fit(cov_type='HC1')
m4 = smf.ols('ln_price ~ distance + dist_b1 + dist_b4 + rating + rating_b35 + C(stars)', data=hotels).fit(cov_type='HC1')
```
:::

```{python}
#| output: asis
def _stars(p):
    return "***" if p < 0.01 else "**" if p < 0.05 else "*" if p < 0.1 else ""
_rows = [('distance', 'Distance (first mile)'), ('dist_b1', 'Change in slope after 1 mile'), ('dist_b4', 'Change in slope after 4 miles'),
         ('rating', 'Rating (up to 3.5)'), ('rating_b35', 'Change in slope above 3.5'),
         ('C(stars)[T.3.5]', '3.5 stars'), ('C(stars)[T.4.0]', '4 stars')]
print("| | (1) | (2) | (3) | (4) |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|")
for _n, _lab in _rows:
    print(f"| {_lab} | " + " | ".join(f"{m.params[_n]:.3f}{_stars(m.pvalues[_n])}" if _n in m.params else "" for m in hotel_models) + " |")
print("| N | " + " | ".join(f"{int(m.nobs)}" for m in hotel_models) + " |")
print("| R² | " + " | ".join(f"{m.rsquared:.3f}" for m in hotel_models) + " |")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;"}
Outcome: ln(price). Stars show significance, using robust standard errors; the standard errors themselves are left out to keep the table readable.
:::

## What changed as we added variables

```{python}
#| output: asis
_m = hotel_models
print(f"- **Fit:** R² rises from {_m[0].rsquared:.2f} to {_m[1].rsquared:.2f} with the distance spline, {_m[2].rsquared:.2f} with rating and {_m[3].rsquared:.2f} with stars")
print(f"- **The first mile matters most:** within a mile of the centre, prices fall by about {abs(_m[1].params['distance']):.2f} log points per mile, far more than the single straight line's {abs(_m[0].params['distance']):.2f}")
print(f"- **Some of that is quality:** add rating and stars and the first-mile slope shrinks to {abs(_m[3].params['distance']):.2f}. Central hotels also tend to be better rated, so the simpler model was giving distance credit for quality. That's omitted variable bias, in the data we've used since Week 4")
print(f"- **Rating matters above 3.5:** each extra point goes with about {_m[3].params['rating'] + _m[3].params['rating_b35']:.2f} log points higher prices. Only {(hotels['rating'] < 3.5).sum()} hotels are rated below 3.5, so the slope there is too imprecise to say much (p = {_m[3].pvalues['rating']:.2f})")
print(f"- **Stars matter jointly:** an F-test that both star dummies are zero gives F = {hotel_stars_f}, p < 0.001")
```

## Finding the deals: most negative residuals {.smaller}

A negative residual means the hotel costs *less* than the model expects, given its distance, rating and stars:

::: {.big-code}
```{.python}
hotels['resid'] = model.resid
hotels.nsmallest(5, 'resid')[['hotel_id', 'price', 'resid', 'distance', 'stars', 'rating']]
```
:::

```{python}
#| output: asis
print("| Hotel | Price | Residual (ln price) | Distance | Stars | Rating |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for _r in hotel_deals.itertuples():
    print(f"| {_r.hotel_id} | €{_r.price} | {_r.resid:.3f} | {_r.distance:.1f} mi | {_r.stars:g}★ | {_r.rating:.1f} |")
```

::: {.fragment}
This is the payoff since Week 4: not a single fitted line, but a benchmark good enough to say which specific hotels look cheap for what they offer. And the model matters: only `{python} hotel_overlap` of the straight line's five best deals are still on this list.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::
